profile.campus: White Oak Technology Park, Henrico County, Virginia (Meta's Henrico data center campus, near Richmond)
profile.reading:
This Meta data center building (building 2 of 3 mapped in this cluster, westernmost to easternmost ordering) is part of Meta's Henrico campus at the White Oak Technology Park near Richmond, Virginia. The project was first publicly discussed as "Project Echo" in September 2017 and formally announced by Facebook that October, with Facebook committing $750 million directly and total planned investment reported at $1 billion; the first phase totaled 970,000 square feet, with potential full build-out envisioned at up to 2.5 million square feet, per Data Center Dynamics and Data Center Knowledge's contemporaneous coverage. The Henrico facility went online and began serving data in August 2020, supporting 200 long-term jobs and having drawn more than 1,500 construction workers at peak building phases. To supply renewable power, Dominion Energy Virginia created a new tariff, Schedule RF, specifically to let large customers like Facebook fund dedicated Virginia solar generation without shifting costs to other ratepayers; Facebook said it funded 500 megawatts of new Virginia solar capacity to source the Henrico center's power as 100% renewable energy, with strong political backing at the time from Governor Terry McAuliffe's administration. Meta's own current fact sheet for the campus reports LEED Gold certification and Meta's standard net-zero, 100%-renewable, and water-positive-by-2030 commitments. Meta does not publish a specific street address, exact current building count, or per-building square footage beyond the original 970,000-square-foot Phase 1 figure; the address above is derived from reverse-geocoding this building's mapped coordinates, not from an operator-published source, and should be treated as approximate.

Meta has continued expanding at White Oak: in October 2022 it purchased 475 acres at 3951 Portugee Road for $35.3 million under the internal code name "Project Tropical" (following the earlier "Project Echo" naming), more than doubling its White Oak holdings to just over 800 acres, after roughly 326 acres acquired between 2017 and 2020 for about $13.4 million, according to Richmond BizSense's reporting on county planning filings. Conceptual plans filed with Henrico County called for two additional data centers and three auxiliary buildings on the wooded parcel directly south of Meta's existing facility, by then described in county filings as roughly 2.4 million square feet. Henrico's attractiveness for the expansion was tied by that reporting to the area's proximity to transatlantic subsea internet cables landing at Virginia Beach and to the county's decision to cut its data-center tax rate by about 88 percent, to 40 cents per $100 of assessed value.

reading.body:
Meta's Henrico campus near Richmond went live in August 2020 as the first phase of a $1 billion Virginia investment anchored by 970,000 square feet of technical space. Meta does not publish the campus's current IT capacity in megawatts, so its power draw cannot be verified against the state context ranking shown here. The operator committed to sourcing the facility's power from 500 megawatts of new Virginia solar capacity funded directly by Meta under a renewable tariff, Schedule RF, that Dominion Energy Virginia created specifically to enable this project without cost-shifting to other ratepayers. The campus holds LEED Gold certification.

Meta has continued expanding at White Oak: in October 2022 it purchased 475 additional acres, more than doubling its holdings to just over 800 acres total, and filed conceptual plans with Henrico County for two more data centers on the southern parcel. The expansion reflects the site's strategic position near transatlantic subsea cable landings at Virginia Beach and Henrico's 88 percent cut to the data-center tax rate, reducing it to 40 cents per $100 of assessed value. The county's published capacity of 1,375 megawatts across 23 mapped facilities does not include Henrico's power draw because Meta publishes no per-building figure, making its true rank in Virginia unknown.

Henrico sits outside the dominant Northern Virginia cluster and represents Virginia's broader data-center growth inland from Loudoun County. The Schedule RF renewable tariff created for this project was cited as a model other major operators in Virginia, including AWS, Equinix, and Digital Realty, could use for their own renewable commitments, signaling the site's importance to the state's energy-infrastructure strategy for large data centers. Virginia has 326 mapped facilities across the state, but only 23 publish capacity figures, so most capacity remains unquantified in public records.
